author: Charles Perrault (1628-1703) - French author, member Académie française, father of literary fairy tale
year: 1691-1697 - Histoires ou contes du temps passé, avec des moralités - Contes de ma Mère l'Oye (Mother Goose)
famous_firsts: First literary Cinderella with glass slipper
note: Perrault wrote 8 prose fairy tales in 1697 collection (Tales of Mother Goose) plus 3 verse tales earlier. All 11 included here with full texts public domain.

stories.title: La Belle au bois dormant - Sleeping Beauty in the Wood
stories.full_story: There once was a king and queen who longed for child, at last queen bore daughter. Christening, invited seven fairies as godmothers giving gifts: beauty, wit, grace, dance, song etc. Old fairy not invited for 50 years in tower thought dead, appears angry, curses: princess shall pierce hand with spindle and die. Youngest fairy mitigates: not die but sleep 100 years until prince awakens. King bans spindles. At 15 or 16, princess wandering castle finds old woman spinning, pricks finger, falls asleep, fairy puts all castle to sleep, forest of thorns grows. After 100 years, prince from another kingdom hunts, hears tale, cuts through thorns (they open for him). Finds princess sleeping beautiful, kneels, she awakens, whole castle awakens. Prince marries. But prince's mother is ogress who wants to eat children? In Perrault's extended version, they have two children Dawn (Aurore) and Day (Jour), ogress mother-in-law tries to have steward cook them with Sauce Robert, steward substitutes animals, finally ogress tries to throw queen and children into vat of vipers, but king returns and ogress throws herself in. Moral: No woman waits so long for husband without trouble but tale says marriage still happy.
stories.moral: Virtue and patience rewarded, but second part warns of cruel in-laws
stories.source: Perrault - Histoires ou contes du temps passé - 1697

stories.title: Le Petit Chaperon rouge - Little Red Riding Hood
stories.full_story: There was once a little village girl, prettiest ever seen, mother and grandmother doted, grandmother made red hood (chaperon), called Little Red Riding Hood. Mother sends her with cake and pot of butter to grandmother sick in other village. Girl goes through wood, meets wolf who wants to eat her but fears woodcutters nearby. Wolf asks where going, girl tells. Wolf says I go this way you that way, see who arrives first. Wolf runs short way, arrives, kills grandmother, eats her (in some versions), puts her clothes, lies in bed. Little Red Riding Hood knocks, wolf disguises voice. Girl enters: 'Grandmother what big arms you have!' 'All the better to hug you.' 'What big legs!' 'All the better to run.' 'What big ears!' 'All the better to hear.' 'What big eyes!' 'All the better to see.' 'What big teeth!' 'All the better to eat you!' And wolf eats her. Perrault ends here with moral warning, no rescue. In later Grimm version huntsman saves. Moral: Young girls should not listen to strangers, especially charming wolves.
stories.moral: Don't trust strangers - especially smooth-talking wolves

stories.title: La Barbe bleue - Blue Beard
stories.full_story: There was a man with fine houses and blue beard which made him ugly and frightening, wives disappeared mysteriously. He courts neighboring gentleman's two daughters, younger eventually marries for wealth despite fear. Month after wedding he says must travel, gives keys to wife: all rooms open except small closet at end of gallery, forbids to enter or else wrath. She promises. He leaves. She invites sister Anne and friends, they tour palace, but curiosity overcomes, she opens closet: floor covered in blood, dead bodies of previous wives hung on wall (throats cut). She drops key in blood, blood won't wash off (magic key). Blue Beard returns early, sees blood on key, says you shall join them tonight. She begs time to pray, calls sister Anne on tower to watch for brothers. 'Anne, sister Anne, do you see anyone coming?' 'I see only sun and grass.' Brothers - dragoon and musketeer - arrive, kill Blue Beard, wife inherits fortune, marries worthy man. Moral: Curiosity is dangerous but disobedience in marriage? Perrault gives two morals.
stories.moral: Curiosity killed wives, but also tale of female curiosity and male tyranny

stories.title: Le Maître chat ou le Chat botté - Puss in Boots / Master Cat
stories.original_french: Le Maître chat ou le Chat botté
stories.full_story: Miller dies leaving to three sons: mill to eldest, donkey to second, cat to youngest. Youngest despairs. Cat says 'Give me bag and boots, trust me.' Cat puts boots, goes to warren, puts bran and sow-thistle in bag, catches rabbit, presents to king as gift from Marquis of Carabas (his master). Does same with partridges. Months. One day king drives with daughter princess by river. Cat tells master undress and bathe in river, hides clothes. When king passes cat shouts 'Help! Marquis of Carabas drowning!' King sends clothes, welcomes. Cat runs ahead, tells peasants mowing and reaping to tell king fields belong to Marquis of Carabas or will be minced. Comes to castle of ogre who can transform to any animal. Cat asks to see: ogre becomes lion, cat pretends fear then asks to become mouse, ogre becomes mouse, cat eats him. Castle now his master's. King arrives, sees castle, thinks Marquis rich, Marquis marries princess. Cat becomes great lord who hunts only for amusement. Moral: Industry and know-how worth more than inherited wealth.
stories.moral: Cleverness and audacity can make fortune

stories.title: Les Fées - The Fairies / Diamonds and Toads
stories.full_story: Widow has two daughters: elder like mother, proud and disagreeable; younger like dead father, sweet and beautiful, most beautiful girl, mother hates her, makes her live in kitchen and fetch water twice daily from fountain far. One day at fountain she meets poor woman begging drink (actually fairy). Girl kindly gives, wipes jug, gives. Fairy blesses: At each word you speak, flower or jewel shall fall from mouth. Mother sees? Then sends elder daughter, who meets fairy disguised as fine lady, elder rudely refuses water, fairy curses: At each word snake or toad shall fall from mouth. Elder returns, mother pleased at first then snakes. Younger son of king in forest hears story, meets younger girl weeping, she speaks roses and pearls, prince falls in love, marries, pays father-in-law? Mother and elder driven out, die miserable. Moral: Kindness rewarded with jewels from mouth.
stories.moral: Kindness and sweet speech are true jewels

stories.title: Cendrillon ou la petite pantoufle de verre - Cinderella
stories.original_french: Cendrillon ou la petite pantoufle de verre
stories.full_story: Gentleman marries proudest woman with two daughters like her. He has daughter of first wife, sweet and good, but stepmother hates her, makes her drudge in cinders, called Cinderella (Cendrillon). Father in wife's power. Prince gives ball two nights. Stepsisters go fine, Cinderella weeps, fairy godmother appears, asks for pumpkin, mice, rat, lizards. Pumpkin to coach, mice to horses, rat to coachman, lizards to footmen, rags to cloth of gold and silver with glass slippers. Warns leave before midnight. Cinderella goes, prince admires, she leaves before midnight first night. Second night stays till midnight, clock strikes twelve, loses glass slipper fleeing. Prince proclaims he will marry who fits slipper. Stepsisters try force foot, fail. Cinderella asks to try, fits, produces second slipper, fairy makes her more beautiful, prince marries, Cinderella forgives stepsisters, lodges them in palace and marries them to two great lords. Moral: Grace and kindness more than fine clothes win.
stories.moral: Grace, kindness and godmother help triumph over envy

stories.title: Riquet à la houppe - Ricky of the Tuft / Riquet with the Tuft
stories.full_story: Queen bears son ugly as possible, with tuft of hair on head, called Riquet of the Tuft. Fairy at birth says he will be very witty and can give wit to person he loves best. In same kingdom, another queen bears two daughters: elder beautiful but stupid, younger ugly but extremely witty. Younger witty mocks elder. Riquet sees portrait of elder beauty, falls in love, goes to meet. Elder weeps over stupidity. Riquet says I can give you wit if you marry me in a year. She agrees, instantly becomes witty and clever. Year passes, she becomes witty, now sees Riquet ugly, tries to avoid. He reminds promise. She says wit not enough, needs to love. He says fairy also gave me power to make person I love beautiful: if you want, I can make me beautiful? She wishes with all heart, Riquet becomes most handsome prince. She marries him. Some say she made him beautiful because love makes see beauty. Moral: What we love appears beautiful and witty because of love.
stories.moral: Love makes witty and beautiful; beauty is in eyes of lover

stories.title: Le Petit Poucet - Little Thumbling / Hop-o'-My-Thumb
stories.full_story: Woodcutter and wife have seven sons, youngest tiny at birth no bigger than thumb, called Little Thumbling (Petit Poucet), but very clever, though thought dull because he listened. Family poor, parents decide to abandon children in forest to not starve. Thumbling overhears, puts white pebbles in pocket, drops to find way back. Parents take them again, this time Thumbling has only bread crumbs, birds eat. Lost in forest, they find ogre's house. Ogre's wife hides them, ogre comes sniffing fresh meat, wants to eat boys, wife says tomorrow. Ogre has seven daughters who are also ogresses. At night Thumbling swaps his brothers' crowns with ogress daughters' crowns (or caps), ogre in dark cuts daughters' throats instead. They flee. Ogre puts seven-league boots and chases. Thumbling steals boots while ogre sleeps exhausted on rock. With boots he runs to ogre's house, tells wife ogre captured by robbers demands ransom, takes all money, returns to parents rich, buys offices for brothers, becomes king's messenger with boots. Moral: Little cleverness beats brute strength.
stories.moral: Cleverness of smallest can save family

stories.title: Griselidis - Griselda (verse tale)
stories.full_story: Prince loves virtuous shepherdess Griselidis, marries her despite courtiers. To test her patience and virtue, he takes away her daughter saying will kill, then son, then says will repudiate her to marry other. Griselidis endures with patience and obedience without complaint. Finally prince reveals children alive, raised well, restores her as wife, praises her virtue. Story of patient Griselda from Boccaccio/ Chaucer tradition, Perrault's verse version moral on wifely patience.

stories.title: Peau d'Ane - Donkey Skin
stories.full_story: Great king with beautiful queen dying makes promise not marry except woman more beautiful than her. Queen dies. King looks, only daughter more beautiful than mother. King, blinded, wants to marry daughter (incest motif). Daughter, advised by fairy godmother Lilac (Fée des Lilas), asks impossible gifts to delay: dress color of sky, color of moon, color of sun, then skin of donkey that excretes gold (king's wealth source). King grants all. Daughter flees wearing donkey skin disguise, Peau d'Ane, works as pig keeper in farm. Prince visits farm, sees her beautiful despite donkey skin through keyhole, falls in love. He asks for cake made by Donkey Skin. She puts ring in cake. Prince chokes? Finds ring, says will marry woman whom ring fits. All try, Donkey Skin's tiny hand fits, she drops donkey skin revealing dress color of sun, marries prince. Donkey skin version of Catskin 510B. Moral: Virtue triumphs over desperate father.
stories.moral: Virtue and modesty survive even in donkey skin

stories.title: Les Souhaits ridicules - The Ridiculous Wishes
stories.full_story: Jupiter appears to poor woodcutter in forest granting three wishes. Woodcutter goes home, tells wife. Wife says wish riches. While discussing by fire, woodcutter idly says 'I wish we had sausage.' Immediately sausage appears on nose? Actually in Perrault: wife wishes sausage? Versions: wife says wish sausage for supper, sausage appears. Husband angry that waste wish, wishes sausage stuck to wife's nose. Second wish wasted. Need third wish to remove sausage from nose, leaving poor as before. Moral: Don't wish foolishly.
